Destruction
de-struk'shun
n. (ruin, undoing; rendering Hebrew shachath and abaddon, Greek apoleia)
From the Latin destructio, from destruo, to pull down. Hebrew abaddon is from abad, to perish, and is used as a name for the place of the dead; Greek apoleia is from apollumi, to destroy utterly — the same root gives Apollyon, the destroyer, in Revelation 9.

Biblical Definition

Destruction is ruin, and Scripture insists it is a destination rather than an accident. Proverbs supplies the best-known diagnosis of how men arrive there: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18) — the sequence is stated as a law, and the fall is the visible part of a collapse that began invisibly in the heart. The Psalter uses the word of mortality under God's hand: “Thou turnest man to destruction; and sayest, Return, ye children of men” (Psalm 90:3), where death is not a natural wearing out but a divine word spoken over the race. Paul defines the final sense precisely, and the definition is essential: the disobedient “shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power” (2 Thessalonians 1:9). Everlasting destruction is not a phrase annihilation can hold — a destruction that is over is not everlasting — and the words that follow define it as banishment from the presence of the Lord. Romans traces it to God's sovereign patience: he “endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction” (Romans 9:22), so that even the destroyed are the objects of a longsuffering they despised.

Webster 1828 Definition

Ruin, undoing. Scripture makes it a destination reached by a road — pride goeth before destruction — and defines the final form as everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord.

expand to see more

DESTRUCTION, n. [L. destructio, from destruo, to pull down.] The act of destroying; demolition; a pulling down; subversion; ruin.

2. The state of being destroyed; as, a city given to destruction.

3. Death; murder; slaughter; massacre.

4. Cause of destruction; a consuming plague; a destroyer.

5. In Scripture, eternal death; as, everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, 2 Thess. 1.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 16:18 — "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall."

Psalm 90:3 — "Thou turnest man to destruction; and sayest, Return, ye children of men."

2 Thessalonians 1:9 — "Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power;"

Romans 9:22 — "What if God, willing to shew his wrath, and to make his power known, endured with much longsuffering the vessels of wrath fitted to destruction:"

Modern Corruption

Destruction is read as extinction, and the word is enlisted to prove annihilationism. Paul calls it everlasting and defines it as exclusion from the presence of the Lord, which is a state endured rather than an event concluded.

expand to see more

The annihilationist argument leans on the ordinary meaning of destroy: what is destroyed ceases to exist. But Scripture uses the word for ruin rather than for cessation of being. A ruined garment or a broken vessel still exists; it has been undone with respect to what it was for. 2 Thessalonians 1:9 settles the question by attaching two modifiers that annihilation cannot carry — the destruction is everlasting, and it consists in being from the presence of the Lord. A thing that no longer exists is not away from anything, and a completed extinction is not everlasting; it is instantaneous and then finished.

The principle to recover is that Scripture presents this ruin as the end of a road men walk, not a fate imposed at random. Proverbs 16:18 names pride as the first step, and Romans 9:22 says the vessels of wrath were endured with much longsuffering. Both texts remove any charge of arbitrariness: God is patient with those who are heading there, and the pride that leads them is their own. That is precisely why the warning is preached — while the longsuffering lasts, the road can still be left.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shachath is a pit or corruption, from a root meaning to go to ruin, and abaddon is the place of destruction. Greek apoleia is utter loss or ruin, from apollumi, to destroy.

expand to see more

Hebrew shachath (H7845) — a pit, corruption, destruction; thou wilt not suffer thine Holy One to see corruption.

Hebrew abaddon (H11) — destruction, the place of the dead; from abad, to perish.

Hebrew sheber (H7667) — a breaking, a fracture, ruin; the destruction of the daughter of my people.

Greek apoleia (G684) — utter ruin, perdition; the broad way leadeth to it.

Greek olethros (G3639) — ruin, destruction; the word in everlasting destruction, 2 Thessalonians 1:9.

Usage

"Of the road that leads there: pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall (Proverbs 16:18)."

"Of mortality under God's word: thou turnest man to destruction (Psalm 90:3)."

"Of the final state defined: everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord (2 Thessalonians 1:9)."
